chmmc-2014-team-01.title: Count centerpieces
chmmc-2014-team-01.body:
Call the two tiles of a chunk that touch all the others its *centerpieces*; they are adjacent, and the other two tiles are the two common neighbours of the pair. So each chunk has exactly two centerpieces, and summing over tiles the number of chunks in which the tile is a centerpiece gives $2\times$(number of chunks).

The grid has $37$ tiles: $19$ interior tiles (all $6$ neighbours present), $12$ non-corner edge tiles ($4$ neighbours) and $6$ corner tiles ($3$ neighbours). A tile $T$ is a centerpiece with partner $X$ iff both common neighbours of $T,X$ are in the grid. Interior tile: all $6$ partners work. Edge tile: only the two partners lying inside the grid work (partners along the boundary would need a tile outside). Corner tile: only the middle neighbour works. The sum is $19\cdot6+12\cdot2+6\cdot1=144$, so there are $144/2=72$ chunks.

**Answer: 72**

chmmc-2014-team-01.title: Computer check
chmmc-2014-team-01.body:
Placing the $37$ tiles in axial coordinates and counting adjacent pairs whose two common neighbours are both in the grid also gives $72$.

**Answer: 72**

chmmc-2014-team-02.title: Stella octangula inside a cube
chmmc-2014-team-02.body:
The two tetrahedra are the two tetrahedra inscribed in a common cube (a stella octangula). A regular tetrahedron of side $2$ is inscribed in a cube of side $a=\sqrt2$ (its edges are face diagonals), so its volume is $\frac{a^3}3=\frac{2\sqrt2}3$. Their intersection is the regular octahedron whose vertices are the six face centres of the cube, of volume $\frac{a^3}6=\frac{\sqrt2}{3}$. By inclusion-exclusion the union has volume $2\cdot\frac{2\sqrt2}3-\frac{\sqrt2}3=\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $\sqrt2$**

chmmc-2014-team-02.title: Tetrahedron plus four caps
chmmc-2014-team-02.body:
Each edge of the first tetrahedron touches the second tetrahedron at its midpoint, so the union is the first tetrahedron with four small tetrahedra attached to its faces (each is similar to the original, with half the side length, so $\frac18$ of its volume). The union is $1+4\cdot\frac18=\frac32$ times one tetrahedron: $\frac32\cdot\frac{2\sqrt2}3=\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $\sqrt2$**

chmmc-2014-team-03.title: Count edges two ways
chmmc-2014-team-03.body:
Each friendship (an edge between two people) appears in the graphs of the four people who are neither of its endpoints, so it is drawn exactly $4$ times. Counting the edges in the six pictures: $7,8,8,6,6,9$ (the first graph has $7$ edges), a total of $44=4\times11$, so the group has $11$ friendships in all. Sue's own graph (the first one) shows all friendships that do not involve her: $7$ of them. So she is in $11-7=4$ friendships.

**Answer: 4**

chmmc-2014-team-04.title: Telescoping the product
chmmc-2014-team-04.body:
Let $a_n=b_1b_2\cdots b_n$. Then $a_{n+1}=a_nb_{n+1}=a_n+\dfrac1{n(n+1)}=a_n+\dfrac1n-\dfrac1{n+1}$ and $a_1=1$. Telescoping, $a_n=1+\left(1-\frac1n\right)=2-\frac1n$. Hence $b_n=\dfrac{a_n}{a_{n-1}}=\dfrac{2-1/n}{2-1/(n-1)}$ and $$b_{12}=\frac{23/12}{21/11}=\frac{23\cdot11}{12\cdot21}=\frac{253}{252}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{253}{252}$**

chmmc-2014-team-05.title: Count agreeing pairs
chmmc-2014-team-05.body:
On one question the $15$ students split among $5$ answers; the number of pairs of students who agree on that question is at least $5\binom32=15$ (it is smallest when the groups are as equal as possible, $3$ each, by convexity). Over $q$ questions there are at least $15q$ agreeing pairs in total, but each of the $\binom{15}2=105$ pairs of students agrees at most twice, so $15q\le210$ and $q\le14$.

Construction: Kirkman's schoolgirl problem gives $7$ ways to split $15$ people into $5$ groups of $3$ so that every pair is together exactly once. Use each of the $7$ splittings for two questions, giving each of the $5$ groups its own answer choice. Two students then agree on exactly the $2$ questions coming from the one splitting that puts them together. So $14$ questions are possible.

**Answer: 14**

chmmc-2014-team-06.title: $T$ is $z\mapsto1/z$
chmmc-2014-team-06.body:
In complex numbers $z=x+iy$, $T(z)=\dfrac{\bar z}{|z|^2}=\dfrac1z$. The side $x=1$, $-1\le y\le1$ is $z=1+iy$, which maps to $\dfrac{1-iy}{1+y^2}$. Subtracting $\frac12$ gives $\frac12\cdot\frac{1-y^2-2iy}{1+y^2}$, which has constant modulus $\frac12$, so the image lies on the circle with centre $(\frac12,0)$ and radius $\frac12$; the endpoints $y=\pm1$ map to $(\frac12,\mp\frac12)$ and $y=0$ to $(1,0)$. So the side maps to a semicircle of radius $\frac12$ bulging outwards. By symmetry the four sides map to four such semicircles on the sides of the square with vertices $(\pm\frac12,\pm\frac12)$. The enclosed area is $1+4\cdot\frac12\pi\left(\frac12\right)^2=1+\frac\pi2$.

**Answer: $1+\dfrac\pi2$**

chmmc-2014-team-07.title: Combine the factors and use base 3
chmmc-2014-team-07.body:
For each $k$ with $A=x^{3^k}+x^{-3^k}$: $(A-1)(A+1)=A^2-1=x^{2\cdot3^k}+1+x^{-2\cdot3^k}$. So $$P(x)Q(x)=\prod_{k=1}^n\left(x^{2\cdot3^k}+1+x^{-2\cdot3^k}\right).$$ Put $y=x^6$; then $x^{2\cdot3^k}=y^{3^{k-1}}$ and the product is $\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\left(y^{3^j}+1+y^{-3^j}\right)$. Expanding, each term is $y^{m}$ with $m=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\varepsilon_j3^j$, $\varepsilon_j\in\{-1,0,1\}$; every integer $m$ with $|m|\le\frac{3^n-1}2$ has exactly one such balanced-ternary representation. So $P(x)Q(x)=\sum_{|m|\le(3^n-1)/2}x^{6m}$: $a_k=1$ if $6\mid k$ and $|k|\le3(3^n-1)$, else $0$.

We need the number of $m\ge0$ with $6m\le3^n$, i.e. $m\le\frac{3^{n-1}}2$, i.e. $0\le m\le\frac{3^{n-1}-1}2$ (the bound $m\le\frac{3^n-1}2$ is automatic). That is $\dfrac{3^{n-1}-1}2+1=\dfrac{3^{n-1}+1}2$ values.

Check: $n=1$: $P Q=x^6+1+x^{-6}$, and $a_0=1$ is the only term with $0\le k\le3$: $1=\frac{1+1}2$ ✓.

**Answer: $\dfrac{3^{n-1}+1}{2}$**

chmmc-2014-team-08.title: Best arrangement
chmmc-2014-team-08.body:
A pyramid (tetrahedron) has $6$ edges, so all six lengths are used. Consider the arrangement where the edge $PS=2$ is shared by the faces $PRS$ with sides $(2,3,3)$ and $PQS$ with sides $(2,5,5)$, and $QR=4$. Then the other faces are $PQR=(5,3,4)$ and $QRS=(3,5,4)$, both right triangles. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $PS$: $MR\perp PS$ with $MR=\sqrt{9-1}=2\sqrt2$ and $MQ\perp PS$ with $MQ=\sqrt{25-1}=2\sqrt6$. In triangle $MRQ$ with $RQ=4$: $16=8+24-2(2\sqrt2)(2\sqrt6)\cos\theta$ so $\cos\theta=\frac1{\sqrt3}$ and $\sin\theta=\sqrt{2/3}$. The pyramid is split by the plane $MRQ\perp PS$ into two pyramids over triangle $MRQ$ with heights $MP=MS=1$, so $$V=\frac13\cdot PS\cdot[MRQ]=\frac13\cdot2\cdot\frac12(2\sqrt2)(2\sqrt6)\sqrt{\tfrac23}=\frac{8\sqrt2}3.$$

To see this is the largest, one checks all assignments of the lengths to edges for which every face is a valid triangle (the length $2$ can only lie in a face with other sides $\{3,3\},\{3,4\},\{4,5\},\{5,5\}$) and computes the volume of each with the Cayley-Menger determinant; the maximum is $\frac{8\sqrt2}3\approx3.771$ (the other valid arrangements give smaller volumes).

**Answer: $\dfrac{8\sqrt2}{3}$**

chmmc-2014-team-09.title: Only central binomial coefficients
chmmc-2014-team-09.body:
Every $n>2$ appears at least twice: as $\binom n1$ and $\binom n{n-1}$. The triangle is symmetric, so entries occur in mirror pairs except for the central entries $\binom{2k}k$. Hence a number occurs an odd number of times only if it is a central binomial coefficient $\binom{2k}k$, and then it occurs $3$ times exactly when it has no other occurrence (the conjecture says the count cannot be $5,7,\dots$, but we can check directly). The central binomial coefficients are $2,6,20,70,252,924,3432,12870,48620,184756,\dots$; $\binom21=2$ occurs only once, and $\binom{20}{10}=184756>100{,}000$. The eight numbers $6,20,70,252,924,3432,12870,48620$ each occur exactly $3$ times (a computer search of all entries up to $10^5$ confirms this).

**Answer: 8**

chmmc-2014-team-10.title: Invariant: $mn$ is a perfect square
chmmc-2014-team-10.body:
If $m_1n_1=m_2n_2$ then $m_1n_1$ is a square iff $m_2n_2$ is. If $m_1/n_1=m_2/n_2=u/v$ in lowest terms, then $(m_i,n_i)=(c_iu,c_iv)$ and $m_in_i=c_i^2uv$, which is a square iff $uv$ is, so again squareness is preserved. Since $1\cdot1$ is a square, every reachable point has $mn$ a perfect square. Conversely every point with $mn$ a square is reachable: it lies on the line of slope $m/n$ through a point $(u^2,v^2)$ with $\gcd(u,v)=1$ (because $mn=c^2uv$ square forces $u,v$ squares), and $(u^2,v^2)$ is joined to $(1,1)$ via $(uv,uv)$ ($u^2v^2=uv\cdot uv$, and $(uv,uv)$ has ratio $1$).

Count the points $(cu^2,cv^2)$ with $\gcd(u,v)=1$, $c\ge1$, all coordinates $\le125$. For the larger square $s^2=\max(u,v)^2$ there are $\varphi(s)$ choices of the other (coprime, smaller) value, doubled for order when $s>1$, and each is repeated $\lfloor125/s^2\rfloor$ times: $$\sum_{s=1}^{11}(\text{number of coprime pairs with max }s)\cdot\left\lfloor\tfrac{125}{s^2}\right\rfloor=125+2\cdot1\cdot31+2\cdot2\cdot13+2\cdot2\cdot7+2\cdot4\cdot5+2\cdot2\cdot3+2\cdot6\cdot2+2\cdot4\cdot1+2\cdot6\cdot1+2\cdot4\cdot1+2\cdot10\cdot1=391$$ (with $s=1,\dots,11$; $s=1$ gives the diagonal, $125$ points). A direct breadth-first search over the $125^2$ points confirms $391$.

**Answer: 391**
